SEC25A-01.explanation: The subject is "Cattle," a plural noun with no -s ending; unlike the mass noun "livestock" in the first sentence, it takes a plural verb. The tense is set by the conditional "provided that the herd's drinking water comes from piped springs," whose present verb states a standing condition, so the main verb must also be present: "are safe." "Is safe" treats "Cattle" like "livestock," which does take "was" in the first sentence. "Were safe" has the right number but copies the past tense of the screening, which clashes with the present condition. "Was safe" copies the first sentence's "was" exactly and fails on both number and tense.

SEC25A-02.explanation: When "each" comes before a compound subject ("Each graft and cutting"), the subject is singular, because "each" makes the plants count one at a time; the plural "trays" right before the blank is inside a prepositional phrase. The before-clause "before the growers recognized the fungus" places the action in the past, so the singular past progressive "was developing" is correct. "Were developing" has the right tense but treats "and" as making the subject plural. "Is developing" has the right number but is present, which clashes with "recognized." "Are developing" is wrong on both counts.

SEC25A-03.explanation: The subject is the singular "comparison"; the numeral in "twelve-week" and the plural "candidates" in the of-phrase do not change its number, even though vaccines can also be halted. The time phrase "on the third day of that year's monsoon" names a single finished day in the past ("that year" points back), so the simple past is required: "was halted." "Has been halted" has the right number, but the present perfect cannot take a definite past time phrase. "Were halted" agrees with "candidates," which could be halted in meaning but is not the subject. "Have been halted" is wrong on both number and tense.

SEC25A-04.explanation: The though-clause leaves out a verb phrase, and the only one it can stand for is "withstood three such summers without a blemish," the main clause's present perfect; so the auxiliary must be "have": the cultivars "have not [withstood ...]." Its subject is the plural "cultivars"; "it" just before the blank is the object inside the relative clause "that replaced it," so the plural "have not" is correct. "Has not" agrees with "it" and the singular "russet." "Do not" and "does not" would stand for a simple-present verb such as the first sentence's "spreads," which cannot be what the cultivars fail to do; "does not" is also singular.

SEC25A-05.explanation: The subject of the main clause is the plural "nurses"; "program" right before the blank belongs to the phrase "from the mainland hospital's outreach program," so the verb is "have moved." The refrigerator is the one that had to leave the flooding building, so it belongs to "the district's lone health clinic," and the possessive is the singular "its." "Have moved their" has the right verb but gives the refrigerator to the nurses, who came from the mainland and were not flooded. "Has moved its" agrees the verb with "program." "Has moved their" is wrong on both.

SEC25A-06.explanation: The subject of the second clause is the plural "health workers"; "district" right before the blank is the object of "in," so the verb is "carry." What they carry without refrigeration to villages with no electricity can only be the one heat-stable product, "The cholera vaccine," so the object pronoun is the singular "it." "Carry them" has the right verb but points to "the three oral vaccines," two of which, the last sentence says, need cold boxes. "Carries it" agrees the verb with "district." "Carries them" is wrong on both.

SEC25A-07.explanation: The subject is the singular "dermatitis"; "usually a handful of scaly patches on the wrists" is an appositive set off by commas that renames it, so it does not make the subject plural. The verb that completes the clause is "recurred," eight words after the blank, and that intransitive past participle needs the perfect auxiliary: "has ... rarely if ever recurred." "Is" reads well as far as "is in the clinic's experience rarely" (as in "rarely serious"), but "is recurred" is not grammatical. "Have" is the right auxiliary but agrees with "a handful of scaly patches." "Are" fails on both.

SEC25A-08.explanation: The first sentence establishes that blood came from all four barns, so there are four sets of samples, and the phrase "drawn in the barn nearest the duck pond" is needed to say which set the laboratory retested. A restrictive modifier takes no punctuation. A comma or a dash before "drawn" would mark the phrase as extra information about all the samples, implying that every sample came from that one barn, which contradicts the first sentence. A comma after "drawn" separates the participle from the phrase that completes it.

SEC25B-01.explanation: The subject is "atlas," a singular noun whose singular form simply ends in -s (its plural is "atlases"); "dust trails" is the object of "of" and does not govern the verb. The conditional's finite verb is the present "turns" in "if a fragment that the survey cameras logged turns out to stray"; "logged" belongs to a relative clause inside it and does not set the tense. A present condition about what happens whenever a fragment strays requires a present result, "is revised." "Are revised" treats "atlas" as plural because of its -s ending and the adjacent "trails." "Was revised" takes its tense from "logged" and pairs a past result with the present "turns." "Were revised" is wrong on both counts.

SEC25B-02.explanation: The subject is the plural "mains"; "from the reservoir to the hilltop hospital" describes their route, so the singular "hospital" just before the blank does not govern the verb. The phrase "at the height of last winter's cold snap" fixes a single finished stretch of the past, and a present perfect cannot take a definite past time adverbial, so the past progressive "were losing" is required. "Was losing" agrees with "hospital." "Have been losing" has the right number and reads naturally beside the present "is replacing," but the definite past phrase rules out the present perfect. "Has been losing" is wrong in both number and tense.

SEC25B-03.explanation: The subject is the singular "seismometer"; "that recorded the region's strongest aftershocks" is a relative clause modifying it, and "aftershocks" is that clause's object, so it does not govern the verb. The while-clause's finite verb is the present "sort," which arrives only after the participial phrase "puzzled by a slow drift in its readings"; calibration happening during that present sorting-out must be the present progressive "is being calibrated." "Are being calibrated" agrees with "aftershocks." "Was being calibrated" follows the past "struck," "recorded" and "puzzled," but a past progressive cannot run alongside the present "sort." "Were being calibrated" is wrong in both number and tense.

SEC25B-04.explanation: The verb belongs to the second clause, whose subject, placed after the fronted phrase "on ridges above the older craters," is the plural "teams"; "from two universities" only says where they come from, so the verb is "are sampling." The pronoun names the source of the emissions, and the first clause establishes that the only source erupting is "The island's lone active vent, a cinder cone," a singular noun; the older craters are not active, so the emissions are not theirs. The pronoun is "its." "Is sampling its" lets the singular vent and its "has begun" set the verb too. "Are sampling their" copies the verb's plural into the pronoun and gives the emissions to the craters. "Is sampling their" reverses both numbers.

SEC25B-05.explanation: The although-clause omits a verb phrase that the main clause supplies: the geyser does not "discharge water at a nearly constant rate." The main clause's finite verb is "discharge," not "scattered": "scattered along the southern terraces" is a participial phrase describing the springs. Because "discharge" is a present lexical verb and the although-clause's subject is the singular "geyser," the ellipsis takes "does not." "Do not" agrees with the plural "springs" instead. "Was not" and "were not" would require an omitted adjective or participle after be, but the omitted predicate is "discharge water," and both clash with the present "discharge"; "were not" is also plural.

SEC25B-06.explanation: The subject is the singular "glare"; "off one solar farm's panels" says where it comes from, so the plural "panels" before the blank does not govern the verb. The each-time clause's finite verb is the past "struck"; "track" belongs to the relative clause "that the airport's planners track in their models," which describes the sun and does not set the tense. A repeated past event requires a past main verb: "was dangerous." "Were dangerous" agrees with "panels." "Is dangerous" copies the present "track" and the present rule in the first sentence, but cannot pair with "struck." "Are dangerous" is wrong in both number and tense.

SEC25B-07.explanation: The subject is the compound "a technician and two engineers," which is plural even though its first noun is singular, so the verb is "were covering." The object pronoun refers to what the opening purpose phrase says must be kept from warping, "a mountaintop observatory's main radio dish," a singular noun, so the pronoun is "it." "Was covering it" lets the singular "technician" and the singular dish set the verb. "Were covering them" copies the plural subject's number into the pronoun, as though the crews were covering the wind farms. "Was covering them" reverses both numbers.

SEC25B-08.explanation: The words after the blank begin a second independent clause: its subject is "a crescent of bare rock rising above the debris field," and its verb, "drew," arrives ten words later; "rising" is only a participle inside the subject. Two independent clauses with no conjunction need a semicolon. The comma makes "a crescent of bare rock" look like an appositive renaming "scar," but once "drew" appears the result is a comma splice. The colon would present the second clause as an explanation or elaboration of the scar, but drawing climbers a decade later is a later event, not a description of the scar. With no mark, the two clauses run together as a fused sentence.

SEC25C-01.explanation: The subject is the compound "the fresco and the gilded screen," two things joined by "and," so it is plural; "chancel," the noun just before the blank, is the object of "of," and "chapel" and "end" belong to the opening phrase. The tense is set by the condition "unless the candles lit in the nave each evening are moved": its verb is the present "are moved" ("lit" is only a participle describing the candles), so the main verb must be present: "are blackening." "Is blackening" agrees with "chancel" or with "fresco" alone rather than with the compound. "Was blackening" and "were blackening" follow the past verbs of the first sentence and the participle "lit," but a past main verb cannot stand with the present-tense condition "are moved."

SEC25C-02.explanation: The subject of the second clause is the singular noun "rivalry"; "bands" is the object of "among," and "contest" and "mills" belong to the first clause. The time clause "after the judges have read out the final scores" uses the present perfect, which in an after-clause marks a present, repeated event, so the main verb must be present: "is reported." "Are reported" agrees with "bands" (or with "weeklies") rather than with "rivalry." "Was reported" and "were reported" follow the past "outlived" in the first clause, but a past main verb cannot be paired with the present-perfect "have read out" in the time clause.

SEC25C-03.explanation: The subject is the singular noun "portrait"; "the two sisters" names its makers inside the phrase "by the two sisters," and "work" and "master" belong to the opening phrase. The time phrase "during the decades after the painters' deaths" names a finished period, since the sisters worked in the seventeenth century, so the verb must be the simple past: "was obscure." "Were obscure" agrees with "sisters" rather than with "portrait." "Has been obscure" and "have been obscure" use the present perfect, which cannot be paired with a closed past period introduced by "during"; "have been obscure" is also plural.

SEC25C-04.explanation: Two decisions are needed. The subject is "the townspeople," a plural noun even though it has no -s (like "people" itself), so the verb is "were"; "cathedral" and "question" are inside the opening phrase. The possessive names whom the townspeople defended: the cathedral and its porch, so it is the singular "its." "Was its" treats "the townspeople" as a single body, like "the town." "Were their" and "was their" would make the townspeople the defenders of a plural owner, but the only other plural, "the canons," is the group they opposed, and the townspeople cannot be their own defenders.

SEC25C-05.explanation: Two decisions are needed. The subject of the main clause is the singular "restorer"; the plural "frescoes" belongs to the because-clause, and the appositive "a specialist in medieval wall painting" only renames the restorer, so the verb is "has uncovered." What was hidden under whitewash, and so what is uncovered, is the plural "frescoes," so the pronoun is "them." "Have uncovered them" makes the verb agree with "frescoes." "Has uncovered it" and "have uncovered it" take "it" from a singular noun such as "wall painting" or "apse," but "wall painting" here names the restorer's field rather than any particular painting, and the apse was never hidden.

SEC25C-06.explanation: The second clause leaves out a repeated predicate, so its auxiliary must be the one the first clause supplies, "was structurally sound": the clause means "the remains of the bell tower were not structurally sound," a form of "be." Its subject is "remains," a plural noun ("the remains were") even though it looks like a verb; "tower" is the object of "of," and "nave" is the other clause's subject. So the verb is "were not." "Was not" copies "was" without changing its number and agrees with "tower." "Has not" and "have not" would need "been" to recover "structurally sound," because the first clause has no form of "have" for them to stand in for.

SEC25C-07.explanation: Two decisions are needed. The verb's subject is the singular "chapel," so the verb is "was visited"; "stalls," the plural noun just before the blank, is inside the phrase "beneath the choir stalls." The agent after "by" is whoever visited the chapel once a year, the plural "monks" of the first clause, so the pronoun is "them." "Were visited by them" makes the verb agree with "stalls." "Was visited by it" and "were visited by it" take "it" from "choir," but in "choir monks" and "choir stalls" the word "choir" only modifies another noun and cannot serve as an antecedent; "church" and "office" cannot visit anything.

SEC25C-08.explanation: The word before "work" must show possession, and the first sentence shows that two copyists wrote the parts: the set "shows two distinct hands," neither the composer's. Their joint work therefore takes the plural possessive "copyists'." "Copyist's" is a singular possessive; it echoes "a hired copyist" and "one scholar's," but it would credit the work to one copyist when two hands wrote it. "Copyists" is a plain plural, which turns "the copyists work on the final chorus" into a subject and verb and leaves "was done" without a subject. "Copyist" is a plain singular that neither marks possession nor matches the two hands.

SEC25D-01.explanation: The subject of the second clause is "the elderly," an adjective used as a noun for a group of people, which takes a plural verb even though it has no -s. The blank elides the main predicate of the parallel first clause, "Renters ... are eligible," so the repeated auxiliary must be a form of be: "are not." "is not" treats "the elderly" as a singular mass noun. "has not" and "have not" copy the auxiliary of "if a landlord has registered the unit," but that verb sits in a subordinate condition about landlords, not in the predicate that the elderly are being contrasted with.

SEC25D-02.explanation: The verb's subject is the singular "eye tracker," which follows the fronted phrase "behind a one-way mirror," so the verb is "follows." The possessive refers to the "infants" at the end of the first clause, the only owners of eyes in the sentence, so it must be plural: "follows their." "follows its" lets the pronoun copy the verb's subject or the nearby "mirror," but neither a tracker nor a mirror has eyes. "follow their" takes a plural verb from "puppets" and "infants" in the first clause, and "follow its" pairs a plural verb with the singular "tracker" and a singular pronoun with the plural "infants."

SEC25D-03.explanation: The words after the colon, "which language should the merged school teach," form a direct question: the auxiliary "should" comes before the subject "the merged school." A direct question ends with a question mark, and the next sentence begins with a capital: "teach? Most." "teach. Most" would suit only an indirect question with statement word order ("which language the merged school should teach"). "teach most" makes "most parents" look like the object of "teach" and leaves "favored" with no subject, and "teach, most" joins two independent clauses with only a comma.

SEC25D-04.explanation: The subject is the plural "applications"; "employer" is the object of the phrase "from the county's largest employer" and does not govern the verb, so the verb must be plural. The opening condition "If outdated forms reached the front desk during the filing season" describes a habitual past practice with the past verb "reached," which requires a simple past main verb: "were routed." "have been routed" has the right number but sets a present perfect against a past condition. "was routed" takes its number from "employer," and "has been routed" carries on the singular perfect of the first sentence's "has been held up"; both are singular for a plural subject.

SEC25D-05.explanation: The subject is "berth assignments," which is plural; "the harbor commission's charter" sits inside the opening phrase "Under the harbor commission's charter" and cannot be the subject, so the verb must be plural. The condition "unless the full council, meeting each spring in the old customs hall, voted to make the arrangement permanent" uses the past "voted," which frames a habitual past arrangement and requires the simple past "were provisional." "have been provisional" has the right number but pairs a present perfect with a past condition. "was provisional" takes its number from the singular "charter" that opens the sentence, and "has been provisional" treats the assignments as the singular "arrangement" named in the condition; both are singular for a plural subject.

SEC25D-06.explanation: The verb's subject is the singular "archivist," so the verb is "is converting." The object pronoun refers to the "hundreds of reel-to-reel tapes" that the linguists left, the only things in the sentence that can be converted into digital files, so it must be plural: "is converting them." "is converting it" takes its number from "trunk" or "catalog," but a trunk is a container and a catalog is the destination. "are converting them" takes a plural verb from "Field linguists" and "tapes" in the first clause, and "are converting it" is wrong on both counts.

SEC25D-07.explanation: The verb's subject is the singular "bookkeeper," separated from the blank by the appositive "a former schoolteacher with little faith in the new technology," so the verb is "was entering." The possessive refers to the "borrowers" of the first clause, the only people in the sentence whose names and payment amounts are recorded, so it must be plural: "was entering their." "was entering its" points the pronoun at "technology" or "lender," but neither has names to enter. "were entering their" takes a plural verb from "borrowers" and "months" in the first clause, and "were entering its" is wrong on both counts.

SEC25D-08.explanation: The first sentence says that during the twelve years "voters never changed mayors," so one person held the office throughout and owned the stadium plans; the singular possessive "mayor's" is required. "mayors'" would be right only if several mayors had made the plans, and the word "mayors" and the twelve-year span tempt that reading. "mayor" lets "the mayor plans for a riverfront stadium" read as a clause, but then "kept" has no subject, and "mayors" is a plural with no possessive mark that also fails to agree with "plans" read as a verb.
